ratings.why: Bad FEN input is likely in real use and a careful builder gives a predictable, catchable error rather than a crash or wrong move list, but nothing that worked breaks and no data is lost.
The request defines a position as a FEN string, which has six fields; accepting the four-field EPD form is a convenience a reasonable builder could skip.

Rejecting anything that is not one of the listed UCI strings is the natural reading, and silently auto-queening 'e7e8' or accepting 'e2e4q' would change games unseen, so a careful builder pins this down.
An exported error class that does not extend Error, or cannot be caught with instanceof, breaks ordinary error handling and is a plain defect anyone would report.
Stale castling or en-passant flags in imported FENs can yield moves of missing pieces and corrupted boards, a real cost a careful builder guards against or documents.
The request fixes status to four values and names only stalemate as a draw, so leaving the fifty-move rule, insufficient material and repetition out is a faithful reading, not a defect.
The request asks for correct move generation for all rules, and pin, en-passant discovered-check, castling-rights-on-capture or promotion-capture bugs are plain defects whatever depth exposes them.
The speed limits are stated requirements, so a careful builder names the position and procedure and guards them, though an unguarded limit costs less than a wrong rule.

The request explicitly asks the tests to cover these named games and rules, so a suite that mentions them without asserting the results (for example the final checkmate) fails the request and leaves the rules unguarded.
The request asks for no documentation and the API is four small functions plus an error class, so a README or doc comments is nice but optional.
The API takes a FEN and returns a FEN, so any hidden state between calls or a board mutated by a rejected move would give wrong answers, a plain defect.
Tests of the error contract keep IllegalMoveError and invalid-input behaviour from regressing silently, a real but secondary safety net beyond the requested rule tests.
